summary: Patrick Löber introduces the concept of any-to-any multimodal agents using Gemini's ecosystem. While the vision suggests one unified model, the current reality involves separate specialized models: the main Gemini series handles multimodal understanding but outputs only text, while native generation models like Nano Banana handle image generation and separate models handle speech. The session focuses on four pillars: multimodal understanding, native image generation, native speech generation, and the Live API for real-time interaction. The flagship example is a NotebookLM clone built as an agent rather than a hardcoded workflow. The architecture has two phases: Phase 1 performs multimodal understanding by ingesting PDFs, images, video, and audio; Phase 2 runs an agentic loop where Gemini acts as a reasoning model, using function calling to invoke specialized generation models. Implementation is straightforward with the Google AI SDK—upload files via the File API or use inline data, combine everything in a contents list, and call generate_content. Practical tips include using Flash for audio transcription, knowing that one minute of audio equals 1920 tokens (yielding 9+ hours of audio within the 1M token limit), leveraging context caching for 90% cost savings, and using timestamp-based analysis. Native image generation (Nano Banana 2, internally Gemini 3.5 flash image preview) inherits Gemini's world understanding—enabling tasks like drawing arrows on a map to generate the Golden Gate Bridge, or correcting math homework on images. Speech generation supports multilingual output with accent and tone control, including two-speaker podcast-style audio. The Live API (Gemini 3.1 flash live) is a true audio-to-audio model with a single architecture and no cascaded pipeline; the demo shows it describing the speaker's appearance in real time. The session closes with shout-outs to a new multimodal embedding model combining all modalities into one unified vector space, and Gemma 4 for local multimodal understanding. Löber emphasizes that the agentic pattern is transferable to every other field.

sections.title: Introduction and Any-to-Any Definition
sections.summary: Patrick Löber introduces himself as a Google DeepMind technical staff member working on Gemini API and AI Studio. He defines any-to-any as Gemini's ability to understand code, image, audio, video, URLs, and Google Search, and generate text, images, speech, video, function calls, and code. He clarifies the current reality: separate models exist (Gemini 3 for understanding with text-only output, Nano Banana for native image generation, speech generation models), with the vision of eventually unifying them. Gemma is mentioned for local multimodal agents.

sections.title: NotebookLM Clone and Agentic Architecture
sections.summary: The goal is to build a NotebookLM clone that ingests multiple sources (PDFs, images, videos, voice memos) and generates podcasts and infographics. The key design choice is building it as an agent rather than a workflow, where a reasoning model decides what to create via tool calls. The architecture has two phases: Phase 1 for multimodal understanding, and Phase 2 for the agentic loop where Gemini reasons, calls tools, and loops until assets are sufficient.

sections.title: Multimodal Understanding Implementation
sections.summary: Implementation is straightforward with the Google AI SDK: get an API key, install the SDK, upload files (PDF, video, MP3) or use inline data, combine in a contents list, and call generate_content with Gemini 3 Flash. Tips: Flash and Flashlight are good at audio transcription; 1 minute audio = 1920 tokens, 1M token limit yields 9+ hours of audio and ~1 hour of video; timestamp-based analysis is supported; File API handles large uploads; context caching saves 90% costs on repeated queries.

sections.title: Multimodal Generation Phase and Function Calling
sections.summary: Phase 2 uses Gemini as the reasoning model in an agentic loop with function calling. Native image generation uses Nano Banana 2 (internally Gemini 3.5 flash image preview), good for infographics. Text-to-speech (based on Gemini 2.5) supports two-speaker podcast-style audio. Function calling requires declaring function name, description, and parameters, configuring tools in the model call, and adding agent instructions to the prompt specifying when to call generate_image vs generate_speech.

sections.title: Why Native Generation Matters
sections.summary: Native generation models are based on Gemini, inheriting its world understanding and training. Examples include drawing arrows on a map to generate the Golden Gate Bridge (not pixel matching but world understanding), and Nano Banana 2 correcting math homework on images and generating code on images.

sections.title: Multi-Language and Accent Capabilities
sections.summary: Audio models are multilingual and understand accents and tone. Demonstrations include a British accent and a Bavarian accent, though not every accent in the world is supported.

sections.title: Live API and Real-Time Interaction
sections.summary: The Live API uses Gemini 3.1 flash live, an audio-to-audio model with a single architecture (audio in, audio out) and no cascaded pipeline. A live demo shows the model conversing in real time, describing the speaker's appearance (short hair, beard, dark jacket, blue shirt). The API can be configured via a Gemini API skill. Users can try it at ai.studio/live.

sections.title: Closing and Additional Model Shout-Outs
sections.summary: Löber notes the agentic pattern is transferable to every other field. He gives shout-outs to additional models announced in the keynote: a multimodal embedding model that combines all modalities into one unified vector space for applications like multimodal search, and Gemma 4 for local multimodal understanding including image, video with native audio. He closes by thanking the audience and encouraging them to build multimodal agents.
